cloze.title: 选词填空 · 远程办公的代价
cloze.text: When offices closed in 2020, many firms assumed remote work would be temporary. Five years later, a {{1}} of employees still work from home at least three days a week. The benefits are obvious: less commuting, lower office costs, and more control over the working day. Yet a growing body of research {{2}} that something is being lost. In a study of twelve thousand engineers, those who worked remotely full-time received feedback twenty percent less often than their office-based colleagues. Feedback, it turns out, is rarely scheduled. It happens in the corridor, in the five minutes before a meeting, in the {{3}} remark of a colleague passing a desk. Firms have tried to {{4}} this loss with weekly video calls, but a call is a reporting event, not a conversation. The result is that junior staff {{5}} slower, not because they lack ability, but because nobody notices when they are stuck. Some companies now require new employees to come in four days a week while allowing senior staff to stay home. That policy may protect short-term productivity, but it risks creating two classes of workers: those who are seen and those who are merely {{6}}. The deeper lesson is that offices were never really about desks. They were about {{7}} knowledge that nobody thought to write down.

cloze.title: 选词填空 · 城市热岛
cloze.text: A city is usually several degrees warmer than the countryside around it. The {{1}} is not mysterious: concrete stores heat during the day and releases it at night, while vehicles and air conditioners add more. This "heat island" effect is not a minor {{2}}; in a severe summer it can double the number of heat-related deaths. The cheapest solution is also the oldest: trees. A mature street tree can cool the air beneath it by as much as five degrees, and it does so without electricity. Yet many cities continue to {{3}} trees for parking spaces, because a parking space produces an immediate income while shade produces a benefit nobody can invoice. Some local governments have begun to {{4}} the two: developers must now plant a tree for every parking space they create. Roofs offer another opportunity. Painting a dark roof white can {{5}} indoor temperatures by three or four degrees, and the paint pays for itself within two summers. None of these measures {{6}} the underlying cause, which is the way cities are built. But they buy time, and time is what a warming climate takes away.

cloze.title: 选词填空 · 语言与思维
cloze.text: Does the language you speak shape the way you think? For decades the question was treated as {{1}} rather than science. Then researchers began to find small but reliable differences. Speakers of languages that divide nouns into genders rate objects differently: a bridge, feminine in German, is described as elegant; the same bridge, masculine in Spanish, is described as strong. Such findings do not {{2}} that language determines thought, only that it nudges it. More striking are the effects on memory. In one experiment, speakers of a language that distinguishes light blue from dark blue by separate words were faster at {{3}} between the two shades. There is an obvious {{4}} for language learning: the more distinctions a language forces you to make, the more attention you must pay to details you previously ignored. This may explain why adult learners often report that a new language gives them a second {{5}} on their own culture. The claim that language is a prison has been {{6}}; the better metaphor is a lens, which sharpens some features and blurs others.

cloze.title: 选词填空 · 食物浪费
cloze.text: Roughly one third of the food produced for human consumption is never eaten. This is not mainly a household problem: in richer countries most waste happens before the food reaches a kitchen. Supermarkets {{1}} fruit that is the wrong shape, and restaurants cook for a demand they cannot predict. The environmental cost is {{2}}: wasted food consumes water, fuel and fertiliser, then releases methane as it rots. If food waste were a country, it would be the third largest {{3}} of greenhouse gases. Some countries now require supermarkets to {{4}} unsold food to charities, a policy that reduces waste and helps food banks at the same time. Others have changed the labels. "Best before" dates describe quality, not safety, yet many consumers {{5}} them as warnings and throw away food that is perfectly good. Removing those dates from long-life products cut household waste in one country by a fifth. None of this requires new technology. It requires the {{6}} to see waste as a cost rather than an inconvenience.

careful.title: 仔细阅读 · 算法推荐的代价
careful.text:
Recommendation systems are usually judged by how well they predict what a user will click. By that measure they are a triumph. But a system that only predicts clicks will eventually show people what they already believe, because agreement is comfortable and comfort is clickable. The result is not that users become stupid; it is that they become narrow.

A recent experiment offers a useful correction. Researchers gave one group of participants a feed ranked by predicted clicks and another group a feed ranked by predicted learning — that is, content that was unfamiliar but likely to be valued later. After six weeks, the second group reported greater satisfaction, spent slightly more time reading, and returned more often. The first group clicked more but described the experience, in interviews, as "empty".

This should not surprise anyone who has watched how taste develops. Nobody chooses to acquire a taste for coffee or for difficult novels on the basis of immediate pleasure. Taste grows because someone reliable told us it was worth the effort, and because the effort itself became interesting. A feed optimized for clicks has no way to represent that process; it can only repeat what we already like.

The practical question is not whether to abandon personalization, which is now technically unavoidable, but what to optimize for. Optimizing for time spent rewards outrage, because outrage is engaging. Optimizing for stated satisfaction rewards comfort. Optimizing for later value requires the system to be wrong about you for a while, which is expensive and, for a company judged quarterly, unglamorous.

Some platforms have begun to report "meaningful" interactions rather than raw engagement, though the definition remains conveniently vague. Until that definition is public and measurable, users will keep receiving what they already wanted, and will keep wondering why they feel bored.

questions.q: What is the author’s main criticism of click-based recommendation?
options: It narrows what users are exposed to.
It is too expensive to run.
questions.explain: 第二段 the result is … they become narrow 是主旨句，其余为支撑。

questions.q: What did the experiment find about the "learning" feed?
options: It produced higher satisfaction and more return visits.
It was disliked by most participants.
questions.explain: greater satisfaction, spent slightly more time, returned more often。

questions.q: Why does the author mention coffee and difficult novels?
options: To show taste develops through effort.
To prove that preference is fixed.
questions.explain: Nobody chooses … on the basis of immediate pleasure，用类比论证。

questions.q: What does "unglamorous" (Para. 4) suggest about optimizing for later value?
options: It is easy to explain to investors.
It is unappealing to companies judged quarterly.
questions.explain: expensive and, for a company judged quarterly, unglamorous，语境指向商业压力。

questions.q: What is the author’s attitude toward current platform metrics?
questions.explain: conveniently vague、will keep wondering 透露保留态度，但未全盘否定。

careful.title: 仔细阅读 · 学历与技能
careful.text:
Employers say they cannot find workers with the right skills. At the same time, millions of graduates hold jobs that do not require a degree. Both statements are true, and the gap between them is not mainly about the quantity of education but about its shape.

A degree signals three things at once: knowledge, the ability to finish something long, and the willingness to follow institutional rules. Employers value the second and third more than they admit, because those qualities are hard to test in an interview. This is why a history graduate is hired for a job in logistics: the content is irrelevant, the signal is not.

The problem is that the signal has become expensive without becoming more informative. When a third of the population holds a degree, possessing one no longer distinguishes anyone; it merely avoids exclusion. The cost of the signal is paid by individuals, while the benefit — a larger pool of disciplined applicants — is collected by employers. Economists call this a positional good: what matters is not how much you have, but whether you have more than the person beside you.

Two developments may weaken the arrangement. First, skills-based hiring, in which employers test specific competences rather than credentials, has spread in technical fields. Second, the supply of graduates in some subjects now exceeds demand so clearly that the wage premium has fallen toward zero. Neither development removes the value of a degree; both reduce its power to sort people.

The sensible response for a student is not to skip education but to notice what the degree does not certify. It does not certify that you can work with someone who dislikes you, that you can explain a complicated thing in three sentences, or that you can recover from a failure you caused. Those are the skills employers describe when they say they cannot find the right people.

questions.q: What does the author say about the gap between employers’ complaints and graduate employment?
options: It is caused by too few graduates.
It concerns the shape rather than the amount of education.
It has been exaggerated by the media.
It will disappear within a decade.
questions.explain: 第一段末句直接给出：not mainly about the quantity … but about its shape。

questions.q: Why do employers hire graduates whose subject is unrelated?
options: Because a degree signals persistence and rule-following.
Because they are cheaper to hire.
questions.explain: the content is irrelevant, the signal is not。

questions.q: What does "positional good" mean in this context?
options: A good whose value depends on ranking against others.
A good that is imported from abroad.
A good that improves with age.
questions.explain: not how much you have, but whether you have more than the person beside you。

questions.q: What effect does the oversupply of graduates have?
options: It reduces the degree’s sorting power.
It ends the need for education.
questions.explain: both reduce its power to sort people。

questions.q: What does the author advise students to do?
options: Recognize what a degree does not prove.
questions.explain: 末段 to notice what the degree does not certify。

careful.title: 仔细阅读 · 城市中的孤独
careful.text:
Loneliness is usually described as a personal problem, a failure to make friends. Public health researchers describe it differently: as a measurable condition with physical consequences, roughly as damaging to health as smoking fifteen cigarettes a day.

What makes the condition interesting is that it does not track population density. Some of the loneliest places measured in Britain are small towns, not tower blocks. What predicts loneliness better than density is turnover — how often the people around you change. A street where half the residents move every year never develops the small obligations that make neighbourliness possible: collecting a parcel, watching a child for ten minutes, noticing that someone has not been out for a week.

This has an uncomfortable implication for policy. Governments have invested in "social infrastructure" — libraries, parks, community halls — on the assumption that shared space produces connection. The evidence is more modest. Shared space produces connection only when the same people use it repeatedly. A park that hosts a weekly market creates neighbours; a park that hosts a different event each weekend creates audiences.

The most effective interventions are embarrassingly small. In one Dutch programme, neighbours were simply asked to sign a card promising to keep an eye on one another’s homes. The card did nothing practical. It created permission to speak, and speaking was the intervention.

None of this means that loneliness can be solved by being nicer. Chronic loneliness often follows bereavement or illness, and no amount of neighbourliness replaces what was lost. But it does mean that the built environment and the social calendar are not neutral. They make some kinds of contact easy and others nearly impossible.

questions.q: How do public health researchers describe loneliness?
options: As a health condition comparable to heavy smoking.
As a temporary feeling of sadness.
As a problem of dense housing.
questions.explain: a measurable condition with physical consequences, roughly as damaging as smoking。

questions.q: What predicts loneliness better than population density?
questions.explain: What predicts loneliness better than density is turnover。

questions.q: What does the author say about shared public space?
options: It works only with repeated use by the same people.
It is a waste of public money.
questions.explain: only when the same people use it repeatedly。

questions.q: Why was the Dutch card programme effective?
options: It gave people a reason to start talking.
questions.explain: It created permission to speak。

questions.q: What is the author’s overall conclusion?
options: Loneliness can be cured by friendliness.
Physical and social settings shape how easy contact is.
Neighbours should be legally obliged to help.
questions.explain: 末段 the built environment and the social calendar are not neutral。

careful.title: 仔细阅读 · 自动化与工作
careful.text:
Predictions that machines will eliminate most jobs have been made for two centuries, and for two centuries the jobs have reappeared in different forms. This history is often used to argue that the current wave of automation will be no different. The argument is comforting but incomplete.

Previous waves replaced physical tasks: lifting, weaving, calculating. The workers affected could often move to tasks that required judgement, because judgement was the one thing machines could not supply. The current wave is different in that it targets judgement itself — reading a contract, diagnosing an image, drafting a summary. When the machine can do the judgement, the remaining human tasks are not automatically better paid; they are often the ones that require presence: caring, persuading, repairing.

Those tasks share a feature that economists have noticed for a long time. They are hard to automate but also hard to scale, because they are performed one person at a time. A software product can serve a million users; a nurse cannot. As a result, productivity growth in these sectors is slow, and wages grow slowly with it.

So the likely pattern is not mass unemployment but a change in the distribution of work: fewer routine cognitive jobs, more personal service jobs, and a smaller number of very highly paid technical jobs. That distribution has political consequences. The middle of the income distribution was built on routine cognitive work; when it shrinks, the argument for redistribution becomes louder and harder to ignore.

None of this is destiny. Countries that invest in training for presence-heavy work, and that treat care as infrastructure rather than charity, will feel the change differently from those that do not.

questions.q: Why does the author call the comforting argument "incomplete"?
options: Because this wave targets judgement, not only physical tasks.
questions.explain: 第三段 The current wave is different in that it targets judgement itself。

questions.q: What characterizes the remaining human tasks?
options: They require presence and are hard to scale.
questions.explain: hard to automate but also hard to scale … one person at a time。

questions.q: Why do wages grow slowly in personal service sectors?
questions.explain: productivity growth in these sectors is slow, and wages grow slowly with it。

questions.q: What political consequence does the author foresee?
questions.explain: the argument for redistribution becomes louder。

questions.q: What is implied about countries that treat care as charity?
options: They may feel the change more sharply.
questions.explain: 末句对比结构：will feel the change differently from those that do not，暗示应对差。

match.title: 长篇阅读 · 大学正在改变什么

paras.label: A
paras.text: Online courses were expected to replace lectures. In practice they replaced the textbook. Students watch short videos before class and spend class time solving problems, a model known as the flipped classroom.

paras.label: B
paras.text: The lecture has not disappeared; it has become shorter and more optional. Attendance at large lectures has fallen by a third in some universities, while demand for small group sessions has risen sharply.

paras.label: C
paras.text: Assessment is the slowest thing to change. Most universities still grade by examination, largely because exams are cheap to administer and easy to defend when grades are challenged.

paras.label: D
paras.text: Employers increasingly ask for evidence of work, not transcripts. Portfolios, project reports and references from supervisors are weighted more heavily than grade point averages in many technical fields.

paras.label: E
paras.text: The cost of teaching has not fallen. Technology has reduced the cost of distributing content, but teaching itself remains labour-intensive, and small groups are more expensive than large lectures.

paras.label: F
paras.text: International student numbers have become financially critical for several systems. A small fall in enrolment can produce a large budget gap, since international fees often subsidise domestic places.

paras.label: G
paras.text: Some institutions now offer micro-credentials: short, verified records of specific competences. Their value depends entirely on whether employers recognise them, which in turn depends on reputation, not on design.

paras.label: H
paras.text: The most consistent finding from research on learning is unglamorous: students learn more when they are asked to retrieve information than when they are asked to review it. Few institutions have rebuilt their programmes around this finding.

statements.s: Exams survive partly because they are inexpensive and defensible.
Employers in some fields value demonstrated work more than grades.
Small classes are more costly than large lectures.
Income from overseas students supports places for local students.
Short competence certificates are only as good as their reputation.
Students benefit more from being tested than from reviewing.
Online material has displaced the textbook rather than the lecture.
Large lectures are attended less, while small sessions are in greater demand.
